target: AG1's claim that AI is beneficial because it makes everyday life more convenient and improves health, education, workplace safety, and accessibility.
objection: Convenience and usefulness do not outweigh the harms of deploying AI at scale: it can displace jobs and suppress wages, create privacy and accountability problems in healthcare, weaken critical thinking in education, reproduce bias against racial minorities, and expand surveillance in workplaces.

target: AG2's claim that AI harms are inevitable because of job loss, medical risk, critical-thinking erosion, bias, and surveillance.
objection: Those harms are not inevitable; they are implementation and governance problems. With retraining, human oversight, auditability, privacy limits, inclusive design, and narrow safety-focused deployment, AI can still deliver net benefits.

target: AG1's assumption that responsible deployment and governance can reliably manage AI risks.
objection: Mitigation is not reliably achievable in practice because incentives and system design push toward broader tracking, weak accountability, cultural dependence on AI outputs, and incomplete bias reduction even when safeguards exist.

target: AG2's claim that incentives and institutions make AI harms effectively unavoidable.
objection: The objection assumes harms are inevitable rather than manageable. Policy can redirect incentives with privacy-by-design rules, legal liability, better educational workflows, and continuous bias evaluation, so AI can still be good if governed properly.

target: AG1's claim that governance and product design can solve AI's harms at scale.
objection: Those fixes are unlikely to work in practice because enforcement usually lags behind adoption, privacy goals conflict with data-hungry AI training and optimization, documentation-based accountability can be gamed, and educational reliance on AI still erodes skills.

target: AG2's claim that safeguards cannot keep up with deployment, so AI is net-bad.
objection: Deployment can be phased and conditioned, privacy-preserving methods can reduce data exposure, accountability can be strengthened with audits and liability, and education rules can preserve learning; therefore the existence of risk does not make AI socially bad.

target: AG1's claim that certification, privacy-by-design, and education rules can make AI safe and beneficial.
objection: These measures fail at market scale: compliance costs favor big firms and increase concentration, model updates make audits stale, and privacy-friendly design conflicts with business models built on personalization and behavioral targeting.

target: AG2's claim that compliance, monitoring, and privacy-friendly architectures cannot work at scale.
objection: Policy can lower compliance costs, require continuous lifecycle monitoring, and enforce purpose limitation and data minimization, so governance can adapt to updates and incentives rather than being defeated by them.

target: AG1's proposed fixes of shared certification, continuous monitoring, and privacy-friendly personalization.
objection: Shared certification risks capture and weak benchmarks, continuous monitoring usually requires more data and therefore more surveillance, on-device privacy is not universally feasible, and market incentives still reward scope creep and broader data use.

target: AG2's claim that monitoring, certification, and privacy-friendly design cannot work in practice.
objection: Monitoring can be done with minimized and aggregated data, independent regulators and third-party labs can prevent capture, hybrid architectures can preserve privacy, and AI should not be abandoned merely because safeguards are imperfect.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-preserving monitoring, independent regulation, hybrid architectures, and better audits can reliably control AI harms.
objection: Even minimized telemetry can still enable re-identification, representative audits miss long-tail bias and unsafe edge cases, and regulators or labs can still be constrained by resource limits and access dependence on vendors.

target: AG2's claim that imperfect privacy controls and oversight are enough to make AI net-bad.
objection: Reidentification risk means privacy controls should be strengthened, not abandoned; edge cases can be attacked with red-teaming and broader testing; and capture can be reduced by diversifying oversight rather than giving up on AI.

target: AG1's claim that lower-risk deployment, human accountability, and better testing make AI good on balance.
objection: Risk-tiering fails when AI components get recombined into other systems, many harms are externalities borne by non-users who did not consent, and even improved privacy still leaves a pervasive tracking ecosystem that undermines social trust.

target: AG2's claim that recombination, externalities, and imperfect privacy show AI is not good for society.
objection: Recombination can be governed at the integration layer with licensing, access controls, and provenance requirements; externalities can be addressed through anti-discrimination, privacy, and labor law; and many useful AI applications do not require pervasive surveillance.

target: AG1's claim that integration-layer governance and existing law can control recombination and externalities.
objection: Licensing and contracts are too easy to evade in downstream reuse, existing laws are often too slow and hard to enforce against bias, privacy leakage, and surveillance creep, and the benefits of AI are more unevenly distributed than the harms.

target: AG2's claim that licensing, enforcement, and targeted mitigation cannot control downstream reuse and harm distribution.
objection: Recombination can be constrained technically and procedurally through gated APIs, provenance tracking, and procurement rules; enforcement does not have to be perfect to reduce harm rates; and uneven harms call for better design and targeted protections rather than abandoning AI.

target: AG1's claim that lifecycle-aware governance can reduce expected harm enough for AI to be good.
objection: The worst harms are hard-to-measure tail risks such as mass misinformation, fraud, manipulation, and trust erosion; provenance does not stop misuse when incentives favor it; and AI concentrates power in the firms controlling models and data, weakening worker and consumer agency.

target: AG2's claim that tail risks and power concentration prevent AI from being socially good.
objection: Tail risks can be mitigated with provenance, source labeling, retrieval/citation requirements, rate limits, human review, and anti-monopoly or public-interest policies; therefore AI can still deliver real benefits when paired with targeted risk controls.

target: AG1's claim that provenance, filtering, human approval, and public-interest policy can adequately control AI's worst harms.
objection: Watermarks and source labels can be removed or degraded, output filters miss unknown failure modes, human reviewers suffer automation bias and overload, public-sector or antitrust responses are too slow, and routine AI use still erodes critical thinking and independent judgment.
